C.4 Spectral reduction and random-matrix asymptotics

Lemma C.1 (Spectral form of the excess risks).

Let

𝚺^≡1n​𝑿⊤​𝑿=𝑼​diag⁡(ν1,…,νd)​𝑼⊤.\displaystyle\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}}\equiv\frac{1}{n}{\boldsymbol{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{X}}={\boldsymbol{U}}\operatorname{diag}(\nu_{1},\dots,\nu_{d}){\boldsymbol{U}}^{\top}. (63)

Then

𝑨=𝑼​diag⁡(a1,…,ad)​𝑼⊤,ai=nσ2​νi+1τ2.\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{A}}={\boldsymbol{U}}\operatorname{diag}(a_{1},\dots,a_{d}){\boldsymbol{U}}^{\top},\qquad a_{i}=\frac{n}{\sigma^{2}}\nu_{i}+\frac{1}{\tau^{2}}. (64)

Writing

𝒅¯0\displaystyle\bar{{\boldsymbol{d}}}_{0} ≡𝑼⊤​δ​𝝁0,\displaystyle\equiv{\boldsymbol{U}}^{\top}\delta{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{0}, 𝑺¯0\displaystyle\bar{{\boldsymbol{S}}}_{0} ≡𝑼⊤​Δ​𝚺0​𝑼,\displaystyle\equiv{\boldsymbol{U}}^{\top}\Delta{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{0}{\boldsymbol{U}}, (65)

the excess risks in Equations 61 and 62 become

ℒ~emp​(t)\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\text{emp}}(t) =12​∑i=1dνi​(d¯0,i2+(𝑺¯0)i​i)​e−2​ai​t,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\nu_{i}\bigl(\bar{d}_{0,i}^{2}+(\bar{{\boldsymbol{S}}}_{0})_{ii}\bigr)e^{-2a_{i}t}, (66)
ℒ~gen​(t)\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\text{gen}}(t) =12​∑i=1d(d¯0,i2+(𝑺¯0)i​i)​e−2​ai​t.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\bigl(\bar{d}_{0,i}^{2}+(\bar{{\boldsymbol{S}}}_{0})_{ii}\bigr)e^{-2a_{i}t}. (67)
Proof.

𝚺^\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}} and 𝑨{\boldsymbol{A}} are diagonalized by the same orthogonal matrix 𝑼{\boldsymbol{U}}. In that basis,

𝑬t=e−𝑨​t=𝑼​diag⁡(e−a1​t,…,e−ad​t)​𝑼⊤.\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{E}}_{t}=e^{-{\boldsymbol{A}}t}={\boldsymbol{U}}\operatorname{diag}(e^{-a_{1}t},\dots,e^{-a_{d}t}){\boldsymbol{U}}^{\top}. (68)

Substituting this into Equations 61 and 62 immediately yields the stated sums. ∎

Assumption C.1 (Self-averaging initialization).

In the large-system limit, assume that the initial mode weights are asymptotically uncorrelated with the eigenbasis of 𝚺^\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}}, so that

d¯0,i2+(𝑺¯0)i​i≈‖δ​𝝁0‖2+Tr⁡(Δ​𝚺0)d\displaystyle\bar{d}_{0,i}^{2}+(\bar{{\boldsymbol{S}}}_{0})_{ii}\approx\frac{\norm{\delta\mbmu_0}^{2}+\Tr(\Delta\mbSigma_0)}{d} (69)

uniformly over ii.

Proposition C.3 (Self-averaged loss formulas).

Under C.1, if

C0≡12​(‖δ​𝝁0‖2+Tr⁡(Δ​𝚺0)),\displaystyle C_{0}\equiv\frac{1}{2}\left(\norm{\delta\mbmu_0}^{2}+\Tr(\Delta\mbSigma_0)\right), (70)

then

ℒ~emp​(t)\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\text{emp}}(t) ≈C0​1d​∑i=1dνi​exp⁡[−2​(nσ2​νi+1τ2)​t],\displaystyle\approx C_{0}\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\nu_{i}\exp\left[-2\left(\frac{n}{\sigma^{2}}\nu_{i}+\frac{1}{\tau^{2}}\right)t\right], (71)
ℒ~gen​(t)\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\text{gen}}(t) ≈C0​1d​∑i=1dexp⁡[−2​(nσ2​νi+1τ2)​t].\displaystyle\approx C_{0}\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\exp\left[-2\left(\frac{n}{\sigma^{2}}\nu_{i}+\frac{1}{\tau^{2}}\right)t\right]. (72)

If, moreover, d,n→∞d,n\to\infty with aspect ratio λ=d/n<1\lambda=d/n<1, then

ℒ~emp​(t)\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\text{emp}}(t) ≈C0​𝔼ν∼MP⁡(λ)​[ν​exp⁡(−2​(nσ2​ν+1τ2)​t)],\displaystyle\approx C_{0}\,\mathbb{E}_{\nu\sim\mathrm{MP}(\lambda)}\left[\nu\exp\left(-2\left(\frac{n}{\sigma^{2}}\nu+\frac{1}{\tau^{2}}\right)t\right)\right], (73)
ℒ~gen​(t)\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\text{gen}}(t) ≈C0​𝔼ν∼MP⁡(λ)​[exp⁡(−2​(nσ2​ν+1τ2)​t)].\displaystyle\approx C_{0}\,\mathbb{E}_{\nu\sim\mathrm{MP}(\lambda)}\left[\exp\left(-2\left(\frac{n}{\sigma^{2}}\nu+\frac{1}{\tau^{2}}\right)t\right)\right]. (74)
Proof.

Replace the mode-dependent prefactors in Equations 66 and 67 by the common self-averaged value from C.1. This yields the finite sums. The Marchenko-Pastur formulas follow by replacing the empirical spectral average with its large-d,nd,n limit. ∎

Theorem C.2 (Late-time asymptotics and grokking delay).

Assume the setting of Proposition C.3 with λ<1\lambda<1, and let

ν±=(1±λ)2,κ=2​(nσ2​(1−λ)2+1τ2).\displaystyle\nu_{\pm}=(1\pm\sqrt{\lambda})^{2},\qquad\kappa=2\left(\frac{n}{\sigma^{2}}(1-\sqrt{\lambda})^{2}+\frac{1}{\tau^{2}}\right). (75)

Then, as t→∞t\to\infty,

ℒ~emp​(t)\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\text{emp}}(t) ∼Kempt−3/2e−κ​t,\displaystyle\sim K_{\text{emp}}\,t^{-3/2}e^{-\kappa t}, (76)
ℒ~gen​(t)\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\text{gen}}(t) ∼Kgent−3/2e−κ​t,\displaystyle\sim K_{\text{gen}}\,t^{-3/2}e^{-\kappa t}, (77)

with prefactor ratio

KgenKemp=1ν−=1(1−λ)2.\frac{K_{\text{gen}}}{K_{\text{emp}}}=\frac{1}{\nu_{-}}=\frac{1}{(1-\sqrt{\lambda})^{2}}. (78)

If the grokking time is defined by the 95%95\% accuracy threshold

ℒ~​(t⋆)=ϵ8,\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}(t^{\star})=\frac{\epsilon}{8}, (79)

then the leading train-generalization delay is

Δ​tgrok≡tgen⋆−temp⋆≃log⁡(11−λ)nσ2​(1−λ)2+1τ2.\Delta t_{\text{grok}}\equiv t^{\star}_{\text{gen}}-t^{\star}_{\text{emp}}\simeq\frac{\log\left(\frac{1}{1-\sqrt{\lambda}}\right)}{\frac{n}{\sigma^{2}}(1-\sqrt{\lambda})^{2}+\frac{1}{\tau^{2}}}. (80)
Proof.

The Marchenko-Pastur density on [ν−,ν+][\nu_{-},\nu_{+}] behaves near its lower edge as

pMP​(ν)∝ν−ν−.\displaystyle p_{\mathrm{MP}}(\nu)\propto\sqrt{\nu-\nu_{-}}. (81)

Write ν=ν−+u\nu=\nu_{-}+u. In Equations 73 and 74, the exponential factor is e−κ​t​e−2​(n/σ2)​u​te^{-\kappa t}e^{-2(n/\sigma^{2})ut}. Hence both integrals are governed by the same edge contribution

e−κ​t∫0∞u1/2e−2​(n/σ2)​u​tdu∝t−3/2e−κ​t,\displaystyle e^{-\kappa t}\int_{0}^{\infty}u^{1/2}e^{-2(n/\sigma^{2})ut}\differential u\propto t^{-3/2}e^{-\kappa t}, (82)

which proves Equations 76 and 77. The empirical loss contains an extra factor ν=ν−+u\nu=\nu_{-}+u, which contributes only the multiplicative constant ν−\nu_{-} at leading order; this yields Equation 78.

To obtain the delay, solve Kt−3/2e−κ​t=ϵ/8Kt^{-3/2}e^{-\kappa t}=\epsilon/8 asymptotically for tt. The subleading t−3/2t^{-3/2} correction is the same for the empirical and generalization losses, so the leading difference between the two solutions is

Δ​tgrok≃log⁡(Kgen/Kemp)κ.\displaystyle\Delta t_{\text{grok}}\simeq\frac{\log(K_{\text{gen}}/K_{\text{emp}})}{\kappa}. (83)

Using Equation 78 and the definition of κ\kappa gives Equation 80. ∎

C.5 Accuracy and uncertainty of the sampled predictor

Proposition C.4 (Exact accuracy of the sampled VI predictor).

Let 𝐰∼qt{\boldsymbol{w}}\sim q_{t}. For a fixed datapoint (𝐱,y)({\boldsymbol{x}},y), define

mt​(𝒙,y)\displaystyle m_{t}({\boldsymbol{x}},y) ≡y−𝒙⊤​𝝁t,\displaystyle\equiv y-{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{t}, vt​(𝒙)\displaystyle v_{t}({\boldsymbol{x}}) ≡𝒙⊤​𝚺t​𝒙.\displaystyle\equiv{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{t}{\boldsymbol{x}}. (84)

Then the residual

rt​(𝒙,y,𝒘)≡y−𝒙⊤​𝒘\displaystyle r_{t}({\boldsymbol{x}},y;{\boldsymbol{w}})\equiv y-{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{w}} (85)

is conditionally Gaussian under qtq_{t}, and for any tolerance ϵ>0\epsilon>0 the empirical and population accuracies are

𝒜emp​(t)\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{\text{emp}}(t) =1n​∑i=1n[Φ⁡(ϵ−mi​(t)vi​(t))−Φ⁡(−ϵ−mi​(t)vi​(t))],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\Phi\left(\frac{\sqrt{\epsilon}-m_{i}(t)}{\sqrt{v_{i}(t)}}\right)-\Phi\left(\frac{-\sqrt{\epsilon}-m_{i}(t)}{\sqrt{v_{i}(t)}}\right)\right], (86)
𝒜gen​(t)\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{\text{gen}}(t) =𝔼p⁡(𝒙)​[Φ⁡(ϵ−𝒙⊤​(𝒘⋆−𝝁t)σε2+𝒙⊤​𝚺t​𝒙)−Φ⁡(−ϵ−𝒙⊤​(𝒘⋆−𝝁t)σε2+𝒙⊤​𝚺t​𝒙)],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{p({\boldsymbol{x}})}\left[\Phi\left(\frac{\sqrt{\epsilon}-{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\top}({\boldsymbol{w}}_{\star}-{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{t})}{\sqrt{\sigma_{\varepsilon}^{2}+{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{t}{\boldsymbol{x}}}}\right)-\Phi\left(\frac{-\sqrt{\epsilon}-{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\top}({\boldsymbol{w}}_{\star}-{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{t})}{\sqrt{\sigma_{\varepsilon}^{2}+{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{t}{\boldsymbol{x}}}}\right)\right], (87)

where mi​(t)=yi−𝐱i⊤​𝛍tm_{i}(t)=y_{i}-{\boldsymbol{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{t} and vi​(t)=𝐱i⊤​𝚺t​𝐱iv_{i}(t)={\boldsymbol{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{t}{\boldsymbol{x}}_{i}, and Φ\Phi is the standard Gaussian CDF.

Proof.

Since 𝒘∼𝒩⁡(𝝁t,𝚺t){\boldsymbol{w}}\sim\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{t},{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{t}), the scalar random variable 𝒙⊤​𝒘{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{w}} is Gaussian with mean 𝒙⊤​𝝁t{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{t} and variance 𝒙⊤​𝚺t​𝒙{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{t}{\boldsymbol{x}}. Therefore

rt​(𝒙,y,𝒘)|(𝒙,y)∼𝒩⁡(mt​(𝒙,y),vt​(𝒙)).\displaystyle r_{t}({\boldsymbol{x}},y;{\boldsymbol{w}})\mid({\boldsymbol{x}},y)\sim\mathcal{N}(m_{t}({\boldsymbol{x}},y),v_{t}({\boldsymbol{x}})). (88)

The formulas follow by evaluating the Gaussian probability of the interval [−ϵ,ϵ][-\sqrt{\epsilon},\sqrt{\epsilon}]. For the generalization expression, use y=𝒙⊤​𝒘⋆+εy={\boldsymbol{x}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{w}}_{\star}+\varepsilon and absorb the label noise into the conditional variance. ∎

Proposition C.5 (Entropy decomposition of predictive uncertainty).

Assume the predictive model

y|𝒙,𝒘∼𝒩⁡(𝒙⊤​𝒘,σε2).\displaystyle y\mid{\boldsymbol{x}},{\boldsymbol{w}}\sim\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{x}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{w}},\sigma_{\varepsilon}^{2}). (89)

Then the predictive entropy decomposes as

ℍ[y∣𝒙,𝒟,t]=𝔼qt​(𝒘)ℍ[y∣𝒙,𝒘]+𝕀t(y;𝒘∣𝒙,𝒟).\displaystyle\mathbb{H}[y\mid{\boldsymbol{x}},\mathcal{D},t]=\mathbb{E}_{q_{t}({\boldsymbol{w}})}\mathbb{H}[y\mid{\boldsymbol{x}},{\boldsymbol{w}}]+\mathbb{I}_{t}(y;{\boldsymbol{w}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}},\mathcal{D}). (90)

Moreover, the predictive distribution is

pt​(y∣𝒙,𝒟)=𝒩⁡(y,𝒙⊤​𝝁t,σε2+𝒙⊤​𝚺t​𝒙),\displaystyle p_{t}(y\mid{\boldsymbol{x}},\mathcal{D})=\mathcal{N}\left(y;{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{t},\sigma_{\varepsilon}^{2}+{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{t}{\boldsymbol{x}}\right), (91)

and the pointwise epistemic uncertainty is

EU​(𝒙,t)=12​log⁡(1+𝒙⊤​𝚺t​𝒙σε2).\displaystyle\text{EU}({\boldsymbol{x}},t)=\frac{1}{2}\log\left(1+\frac{{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{t}{\boldsymbol{x}}}{\sigma_{\varepsilon}^{2}}\right). (92)

Using the explicit covariance trajectory from Equation 42, this can also be written as

EU​(𝒙,t)=12​log⁡(1+𝒙⊤​𝚺∞​𝒙+𝒙⊤​𝑬t​Δ​𝚺0​𝑬t​𝒙σε2).\displaystyle\text{EU}({\boldsymbol{x}},t)=\frac{1}{2}\log\left(1+\frac{{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{\infty}{\boldsymbol{x}}+{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{E}}_{t}\Delta{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{0}{\boldsymbol{E}}_{t}{\boldsymbol{x}}}{\sigma_{\varepsilon}^{2}}\right). (93)
Proof.

The entropy decomposition is the standard identity H⁡(Y∣X)=𝔼​H​(Y∣X,W)+I⁡(Y;W∣X)H(Y\mid X)=\mathbb{E}H(Y\mid X,W)+I(Y;W\mid X). Since both p⁡(y∣𝒙,𝒘)p(y\mid{\boldsymbol{x}},{\boldsymbol{w}}) and qt​(𝒘)q_{t}({\boldsymbol{w}}) are Gaussian, marginalizing over 𝒘{\boldsymbol{w}} gives Equation 91. The differential entropy of a Gaussian 𝒩⁡(0,s2)\mathcal{N}(0,s^{2}) is 12​log⁡(2​π​e​s2)\frac{1}{2}\log(2 \pi e s^2), so the aleatoric term is 12​log⁡(2​π​e​σε2)\frac{1}{2}\log(2 \pi e \sigma_\varepsilon^2) and the epistemic contribution is the difference between the predictive and aleatoric entropies, which yields Equation 92. ∎

Remark C.1 (Late-time accuracy closure).

In the matched interpolation regime, the late-time residual is approximately centered and its variance is controlled by the excess risk:

𝔼⁡[rt2]≈2​ℒ~​(t).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[r_{t}^{2}]\approx 2\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}(t). (94)

Approximating the residual by a single effective Gaussian therefore gives

𝒜emp/gen​(t)≈erf⁡(ϵ4​ℒ~emp/gen​(t)).\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{\text{emp}/\text{gen}}(t)\approx\operatorname{erf}\left(\sqrt{\frac{\epsilon}{4\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\text{emp}/\text{gen}}(t)}}\right). (95)

The 95%95\% grokking threshold used in Theorem C.2 then corresponds to ℒ~​(t⋆)=ϵ/8\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}(t^{\star})=\epsilon/8 because erf⁡(2)≈0.95\operatorname{erf}(\sqrt{2})\approx 0.95.

Lemma C.2 (Trace dynamics of the covariance).

The covariance trace obeys

ddt​Tr⁡(𝚺t)=2​Tr⁡(𝑰d−𝑨​𝚺t).\displaystyle\frac{\differential}{\differential t}\Tr(\mbSigma_t)=2\Tr(\mbI_d - \mbA\mbSigma_t). (96)

In the eigenbasis of 𝐀{\boldsymbol{A}}, if 𝚺t=𝚺∞+𝐄t​Δ​𝚺0​𝐄t{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{t}={\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{\infty}+{\boldsymbol{E}}_{t}\Delta{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{0}{\boldsymbol{E}}_{t} and Δ​si\Delta s_{i} denotes the ii-th diagonal entry of 𝐔⊤​Δ​𝚺0​𝐔{\boldsymbol{U}}^{\top}\Delta{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{0}{\boldsymbol{U}}, then

ddtTr⁡(𝚺t)=−2∑i=1daiΔsie−2​ai​t.\displaystyle\frac{\differential}{\differential t}\Tr(\mbSigma_t)=-2\sum_{i=1}^{d}a_{i}\Delta s_{i}e^{-2a_{i}t}. (97)
Proof.

Taking the trace of Equation 31 gives

ddt​Tr⁡(𝚺t)=2​Tr⁡(𝑰d)−Tr⁡(𝑨​𝚺t)−Tr⁡(𝚺t​𝑨)=2​Tr⁡(𝑰d−𝑨​𝚺t),\displaystyle\frac{\differential}{\differential t}\Tr(\mbSigma_t)=2\Tr(\mbI_d)-\Tr(\mbA\mbSigma_t)-\Tr(\mbSigma_t \mbA)=2\Tr(\mbI_d - \mbA\mbSigma_t), (98)

using cyclicity of the trace. The spectral formula follows by substituting the explicit solution from Equation 42. ∎

Lemma C.3 (Population-averaged epistemic uncertainty).

The exact population-averaged epistemic uncertainty is

EU​(t)≡𝔼p⁡(𝒙)​EU​(𝒙,t)=12​𝔼p⁡(𝒙)​log⁡(1+𝒙⊤​𝚺t​𝒙σε2).\displaystyle\text{EU}(t)\equiv\mathbb{E}_{p({\boldsymbol{x}})}\text{EU}({\boldsymbol{x}},t)=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{p({\boldsymbol{x}})}\log\left(1+\frac{{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{t}{\boldsymbol{x}}}{\sigma_{\varepsilon}^{2}}\right). (99)

Under isotropic Gaussian design 𝐱∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈d){\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{0}},{\boldsymbol{I}}_{d}) and the same self-averaging closure used above,

EU​(t)≈12​log⁡(1+Tr⁡(𝚺t)σε2).\displaystyle\text{EU}(t)\approx\frac{1}{2}\log\left(1+\frac{\Tr(\mbSigma_t)}{\sigma_{\varepsilon}^{2}}\right). (100)

If 𝚺0≺𝚺∞{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{0}\prec{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{\infty}, this approximate epistemic curve is monotonically increasing; if 𝚺0≻𝚺∞{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{0}\succ{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{\infty}, it is monotonically decreasing; and if 𝚺0=𝚺∞{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{0}={\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{\infty}, it is constant.

Proof.

The exact identity is just the average of Equation 92. Under isotropic Gaussian design, the quadratic form 𝒙⊤​𝚺t​𝒙{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{t}{\boldsymbol{x}} concentrates around its trace in high dimension, yielding Equation 100. Because u↦12​log⁡(1+u/σε2)u\mapsto\frac{1}{2}\log(1 + u/\sigma_\varepsilon^2) is increasing, the monotonicity of the approximate entropy curve matches the monotonicity of Tr⁡(𝚺t)\Tr(\mbSigma_t). The explicit solution Equation 42 shows that each spectral mode evolves as ai−1+Δ​si​e−2​ai​ta_{i}^{-1}+\Delta s_{i}e^{-2a_{i}t}, so the sign of Δ​si\Delta s_{i} determines whether that mode increases or decreases. If 𝚺0≺𝚺∞{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{0}\prec{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{\infty}, then all Δ​si<0\Delta s_{i}<0 and Lemma C.2 implies that Tr⁡(𝚺t)\Tr(\mbSigma_t) increases monotonically; the opposite case is analogous, and equality gives a constant curve. ∎

Corollary C.3 (Isotropic initialization).

If 𝚺0=s0​𝐈d{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{0}=s_{0}{\boldsymbol{I}}_{d}, then

1d​Tr⁡(𝚺t)≈𝔼ν∼MP⁡(λ)​[1a⁡(ν)+(s0−1a⁡(ν))​e−2​a​(ν)​t],a⁡(ν)=nσ2​ν+1τ2.\displaystyle\frac{1}{d}\Tr(\mbSigma_t)\approx\mathbb{E}_{\nu\sim\mathrm{MP}(\lambda)}\left[\frac{1}{a(\nu)}+\left(s_{0}-\frac{1}{a(\nu)}\right)e^{-2a(\nu)t}\right],\qquad a(\nu)=\frac{n}{\sigma^{2}}\nu+\frac{1}{\tau^{2}}. (101)

In particular, when 𝚺0=𝟎{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{0}={\boldsymbol{0}},

1d​Tr⁡(𝚺t)≈𝔼ν∼MP⁡(λ)​[1−e−2​a​(ν)​ta⁡(ν)].\displaystyle\frac{1}{d}\Tr(\mbSigma_t)\approx\mathbb{E}_{\nu\sim\mathrm{MP}(\lambda)}\left[\frac{1-e^{-2a(\nu)t}}{a(\nu)}\right]. (102)
Proof.

Under isotropic initialization, Δ​𝚺0\Delta{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{0} is diagonal in every eigenbasis, so the spectral representation of Equation 42 reduces to a scalar mode-by-mode formula. Averaging over the empirical spectrum and then passing to the Marchenko-Pastur limit gives the result. ∎

Proposition C.6 (Epistemic uncertainty of the threshold model).

Define the thresholded success indicator

Zϵ(𝒙,y;𝒘)≡𝟙{(y−𝒙⊤𝒘)2≤ϵ}.\displaystyle Z_{\epsilon}({\boldsymbol{x}},y;{\boldsymbol{w}})\equiv\mathbbm{1}\{(y-{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{w}})^{2}\leq\epsilon\}. (103)

For fixed (𝐱,y)({\boldsymbol{x}},y), the success probability under qtq_{t} is

pt​(𝒙,y)\displaystyle p_{t}({\boldsymbol{x}},y) =Φ⁡(ϵ−mt​(𝒙,y)vt​(𝒙))−Φ⁡(−ϵ−mt​(𝒙,y)vt​(𝒙)),\displaystyle=\Phi\left(\frac{\sqrt{\epsilon}-m_{t}({\boldsymbol{x}},y)}{\sqrt{v_{t}({\boldsymbol{x}})}}\right)-\Phi\left(\frac{-\sqrt{\epsilon}-m_{t}({\boldsymbol{x}},y)}{\sqrt{v_{t}({\boldsymbol{x}})}}\right), (104)

and

Zϵ​(𝒙,y,𝒘)|(𝒙,y,𝒟,t)∼Bernoulli⁡(pt​(𝒙,y)).\displaystyle Z_{\epsilon}({\boldsymbol{x}},y;{\boldsymbol{w}})\mid({\boldsymbol{x}},y,\mathcal{D},t)\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p_{t}({\boldsymbol{x}},y)). (105)

Hence the threshold-model epistemic uncertainty is exactly

EUt(Zϵ;𝒘∣𝒙,y,𝒟)=h2(pt(𝒙,y)),\displaystyle\text{EU}_{t}(Z_{\epsilon};{\boldsymbol{w}}\mid{\boldsymbol{x}},y,\mathcal{D})=h_{2}\bigl(p_{t}({\boldsymbol{x}},y)\bigr), (106)

where h2​(p)=−p​log⁡p−(1−p)​log⁡(1−p)h_{2}(p)=-p\log p-(1-p)\log(1-p) is the binary entropy. In the late-time self-averaging regime,

pt≈erf⁡(ϵ4​ℒ~​(t)),\displaystyle p_{t}\approx\operatorname{erf}\left(\sqrt{\frac{\epsilon}{4\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}(t)}}\right), (107)

and therefore

EUth​(t)≈h2​(erf⁡(ϵ4​ℒ~​(t))).\displaystyle\text{EU}_{\mathrm{th}}(t)\approx h_{2}\!\left(\operatorname{erf}\left(\sqrt{\frac{\epsilon}{4\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}(t)}}\right)\right). (108)
Proof.

The exact success probability is the Gaussian interval probability from Proposition C.4. Conditional on 𝒘{\boldsymbol{w}}, the variable ZϵZ_{\epsilon} is deterministic, so its conditional entropy vanishes. The predictive distribution is therefore Bernoulli with entropy h2​(pt​(𝒙,y))h_{2}(p_{t}({\boldsymbol{x}},y)), and the full uncertainty is epistemic. The closure formula follows from the same effective-Gaussian approximation that relates the residual variance to the excess risk at late times. ∎

Remark C.2 (Threshold uncertainty versus grokking).

The binary entropy h2​(p)h_{2}(p) is maximized at p=1/2p=1/2, so the threshold-model epistemic uncertainty typically follows a non-monotone trajectory: it rises while predictions are ambiguous and then falls as the model becomes confidently correct. Using Equation 107, the peak occurs when

ℒ~​(tpeak)=ϵ4​(erf−1⁡(1/2))2,\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}(t_{\mathrm{peak}})=\frac{\epsilon}{4(\operatorname{erf}^{-1}(1/2))^{2}}, (109)

and numerically

14​(erf−1⁡(1/2))2≈1.10.\displaystyle\frac{1}{4(\operatorname{erf}^{-1}(1/2))^{2}}\approx 1.10. (110)

Thus the peak occurs when the loss is still of order ϵ\epsilon, which is much earlier than the 95%95\% grokking threshold ℒ~​(t⋆)=ϵ/8\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}(t^{\star})=\epsilon/8. Thus the entropy peak and the grokking delay are distinct observables, even though both are controlled by the same slow edge-of-spectrum modes in the Marchenko-Pastur regime.

Theorem C.3 (Delay between threshold-uncertainty peaks).

Assume the setting of Theorems C.2 and C.6, and suppose the empirical and generalization threshold-model uncertainty peaks occur in the late-time regime where Equations 108, 76 and 77 apply. Then

Δ​tEU peak​(λ)\displaystyle\Delta t_{\text{EU peak}}(\lambda) ≡tpeak,gen−tpeak,emp\displaystyle\equiv t_{\mathrm{peak},\mathrm{gen}}-t_{\mathrm{peak},\mathrm{emp}}
≃log⁡(11−λ)nσ2​(1−λ)2+1τ2,\displaystyle\simeq\frac{\log\left(\frac{1}{1-\sqrt{\lambda}}\right)}{\frac{n}{\sigma^{2}}(1-\sqrt{\lambda})^{2}+\frac{1}{\tau^{2}}}, (111)

up to threshold-dependent subleading corrections.

Proof.

For α∈{emp,gen}\alpha\in\{\mathrm{emp},\mathrm{gen}\}, write

hα​(t)\displaystyle h_{\alpha}(t) ≈h2​(pα​(t)),\displaystyle\approx h_{2}\bigl(p_{\alpha}(t)\bigr), pα​(t)\displaystyle p_{\alpha}(t) ≈erf⁡(ϵ4​ℒ~α​(t)),\displaystyle\approx\operatorname{erf}\left(\sqrt{\frac{\epsilon}{4\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\alpha}(t)}}\right), (112)

as in Equation 108. Since h2′​(p)=log⁡(1−pp)h_{2}^{\prime}(p)=\log\!\bigl(\frac{1-p}{p}\bigr), the binary entropy is uniquely maximized at p=1/2p=1/2. Moreover, the map

ℒ~⟼erf⁡(ϵ4​ℒ~)\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}\longmapsto\operatorname{erf}\left(\sqrt{\frac{\epsilon}{4\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}}}\right) (113)

is strictly decreasing in ℒ~\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}, while in the late-time regime Equations 76 and 77 imply that each loss is strictly decreasing for large tt. Hence each late-time uncertainty curve reaches its maximum exactly when pα​(t)=1/2p_{\alpha}(t)=1/2, namely when

ℒ~α​(tpeak,α)=cpeak≡ϵ4​(erf−1⁡(1/2))2,\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\alpha}(t_{\mathrm{peak},\alpha})=c_{\mathrm{peak}}\equiv\frac{\epsilon}{4(\operatorname{erf}^{-1}(1/2))^{2}}, (114)

which is Equation 109.

Now use the late-time asymptotics from Theorem C.2. For each α∈{emp,gen}\alpha\in\{\mathrm{emp},\mathrm{gen}\},

ℒ~α(t)∼Kαt−3/2e−κ​t.\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\alpha}(t)\sim K_{\alpha}\,t^{-3/2}e^{-\kappa t}. (115)

Therefore the peak time satisfies

cpeak=Kαtpeak,α−3/2e−κ​tpeak,α(1+o(1)).\displaystyle c_{\mathrm{peak}}=K_{\alpha}\,t_{\mathrm{peak},\alpha}^{-3/2}e^{-\kappa t_{\mathrm{peak},\alpha}}\bigl(1+o(1)\bigr). (116)

Taking logarithms gives

κ​tpeak,α=log⁡(Kαcpeak)−32​log⁡tpeak,α+o⁡(1).\displaystyle\kappa t_{\mathrm{peak},\alpha}=\log\!\left(\frac{K_{\alpha}}{c_{\mathrm{peak}}}\right)-\frac{3}{2}\log t_{\mathrm{peak},\alpha}+o(1). (117)

Subtracting the empirical and generalization versions yields

κ​Δ​tEU peak≃log⁡(KgenKemp)−32​log⁡(tpeak,gentpeak,emp),\displaystyle\kappa\Delta t_{\text{EU peak}}\simeq\log\!\left(\frac{K_{\text{gen}}}{K_{\text{emp}}}\right)-\frac{3}{2}\log\!\left(\frac{t_{\mathrm{peak},\mathrm{gen}}}{t_{\mathrm{peak},\mathrm{emp}}}\right), (118)

up to o⁡(1)o(1) terms. The logarithmic ratio of peak times is a subleading correction coming from the common t−3/2t^{-3/2} factor, exactly as in the proof of Theorem C.2. Thus the leading contribution is

Δ​tEU peak≃log⁡(Kgen/Kemp)κ,\displaystyle\Delta t_{\text{EU peak}}\simeq\frac{\log(K_{\text{gen}} / K_{\text{emp}})}{\kappa}, (119)

with threshold dependence entering only through the discarded subleading terms. Finally, Equation 78 gives

log⁡(KgenKemp)=−2​log⁡(1−λ),\displaystyle\log\!\left(\frac{K_{\text{gen}}}{K_{\text{emp}}}\right)=-2\log(1 - \sqrt{\lambda}), (120)

and

κ=2​(nσ2​(1−λ)2+1τ2).\displaystyle\kappa=2\left(\frac{n}{\sigma^{2}}(1-\sqrt{\lambda})^{2}+\frac{1}{\tau^{2}}\right). (121)

Substituting these expressions gives Equation 111. Thus the threshold-model uncertainty peak and the grokking delay are different observables, but near λ≃1\lambda\simeq 1 they are governed by the same edge-of-spectrum slowdown. ∎

Appendix D Reproducibility

We summarize here the full experimental specification needed to reproduce the reported results. Across all experiments, we keep the task family, the transformer architecture, and the evaluation protocol fixed, and vary only the quantities explicitly listed.

D.1 Task distribution and sequence construction

Each example is a two-variable modular arithmetic rule

z=(a​x+b​y)mod29,z=(ax+by)\bmod 29,

where (a,b)(a,b) identifies the task and (x,y)(x,y) is the input pair. The arithmetic base, vocabulary size, and modulus are all 2929. The input space therefore contains 292=84129^{2}=841 distinct pairs (x,y)(x,y).

For each experimental setting, we first sample ntaskn_{\mathrm{task}} in-distribution coefficient pairs and then apply a parallelogram augmentation, which expands the in-distribution family to 4​ntask4n_{\mathrm{task}} related tasks, check 10 for details on the augmentation procedure. Out-of-distribution evaluation uses 256256 additional tasks drawn from the complement of the in-distribution set.

Training and evaluation are performed on sequences of 3232 triplets, corresponding to a token window of length 9696. Only the answer token zz in each triplet is supervised, so learning is next-token prediction on answer positions only. The nominal batch size is 10241024 for both training and evaluation. Training uses a virtual in-distribution set multiplier of 10001000 to increase the number of sampled batches per optimization run. Every evaluation reports three splits: in-distribution validation, out-of-distribution training-point evaluation, and out-of-distribution validation-point evaluation.

D.2 Shared model architecture

All methods use the same decoder-only transformer. The backbone has 66 layers, 44 attention heads, embedding width 512512, and feed-forward width 20482048. The vocabulary size is 2929 and the maximum token window is 9696. The model uses LayerNorm with ϵ=10−5\epsilon=10^{-5}, full rotary positional encoding, tied input and output embeddings, and no bias terms in attention, MLP, or output projections. All runs use mixed bfloat16 precision and one accelerator per run.

D.3 Training and evaluation protocol

The default optimization horizon is 100,000100{,}000 update steps. For the largest base task setting, ntask=128n_{\mathrm{task}}=128, the horizon is doubled to 200,000200{,}000 steps. For every validation split we report accuracy, expected calibration error, mean log-likelihood, aleatoric uncertainty, and epistemic uncertainty. Accuracy, calibration, and uncertainty are reported both over all supervised answer positions in the sequence and on the final answer token only.

D.4 Method-specific settings

The MAP baseline is trained with AdamW using peak learning rate 1.5×10−41.5\times 10^{-4}, linear warmup for 10001000 steps from 1%1\% of the peak rate, and cosine decay to 10%10\% of the peak rate. The momentum parameters are (0.9,0.98)(0.9,0.98), the numerical stability constant is 10−810^{-8}, and the gradient norm is clipped at 1.01.0.

IVON uses learning rate 0.50.5, 20002000 warmup steps, the same 1%→100%→10%1\%\rightarrow 100\%\rightarrow 10\% cosine schedule envelope, β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9, β2=0.99999\beta_{2}=0.99999, Hessian initialization 11, clip radius 10−310^{-3}, one Monte Carlo weight sample during training. The effective sample size is set automatically to the number of in-distribution training point pairs multiplied by the effective in-distribution task count after augmentation.

The Laplace model is fit post hoc on the final MAP solution. The approximation is restricted to the last layer, uses a Kronecker-factored Hessian, and sets the prior precision equal to the MAP weight decay (no marginal likelihood optimization). The Laplace fit is always performed on clean in-distribution training data, with full context sequences of 3232 triplets.

D.5 Experiment families

The main MAP study sweeps base task count, training-point fraction, and initialization seed. Specifically, it uses ntask∈{8,16,32,64,128}n_{\mathrm{task}}\in\{8,16,32,64,128\}, ptrain∈{0.3,0.4,0.5,0.6,0.7,0.8}p_{\mathrm{train}}\in\{0.3,0.4,0.5,0.6,0.7,0.8\}, and 4 seeds. The full Laplace study is aligned exactly with this grid, using the corresponding final MAP solutions.

The primary IVON study uses the same sweep axes over base task count and training-point fraction, with 4 seeds. Unless otherwise stated, these runs use the default IVON weight decay 10−510^{-5}, automatic effective sample size resolution, and 100,000100{,}000 optimization steps, with the same 200,000200{,}000-step extension for ntask=128n_{\mathrm{task}}=128.

Inference-time context-length sweeps evaluate context sizes 1,2,…,321,2,\ldots,32 while keeping the trained model fixed. These sweeps use ntask=64n_{\mathrm{task}}=64 and ptrain=0.8p_{\mathrm{train}}=0.8.

Inference-time context-noise sweeps also use ntask=64n_{\mathrm{task}}=64 and ptrain=0.8p_{\mathrm{train}}=0.8, with fixed context length 3232. Noise probabilities range over {0.0,0.1,…,1.0}\{0.0,0.1,\ldots,1.0\}. Corruption is applied only to eligible context answer tokens; the query triplet and evaluation targets remain clean.

D.6 Hardware allocation

All runs use one accelerator per experiment. The main training runs use NVIDIA H200/H100/A100 accelerators while lightweight validation use small H200 MIG partitions. The total computational budget used for the experimental campaign is approximately 12′​00012^{\prime}000 accelerator-hours, splitted roughly equally between development and final runs.
